The original house is preserved, and does not destabilize the rest of the adjoining housing. The house is based on a modular architecture, this is possible by the use of prefabricated materials. This off -site production allows a quick realization once on site, which turns out to be very cheap.The house itself is completely adapted to its inhabitants and personalized to their uses. This is an essential notion in the development of DTP projects: the human being is at the heart. In the Huang house, on a poor area of 15m2, the kitchen and water space on the ground floor, followed by the bedroom on the first  floor. This minimal relationship to space projects the need for sharing and common spaces towards the outside and thus an appropriation of the street. For the Fang house, small front and back outdoor spaces are  created on the plot, the 25m2 house proposes a 1 bedroom housing on one level.

Pictures @peoplesarchitecture : Huang’s houseThe interview is especially based on the analysis of 2 plugin houses:Shenzen's Shangwei Village, province du Guangdong South China, 2018Mrs Fan's house Historic Beijing Hutong, 2016#China #contemporarychinesearchitecture #density #housing #architecture #pao #peoplearchitectureoffice #architectureinterviews #architectinterviews #prefabricated #massproduction #customedarchitecture #context #hutong #history #minimalliving #lightweightarchitecture #prefabricated #prefabricatedhouse

PRODUCTION*Density / Ecological Urbanism (Taillandier Paris)Curator : Marine Fritsch Master 1 @ensa_versailles The project of No. 28 Dayuan Hu Tong, titled «Miniature Beijing», is a transformation project by Atelier Li Xinggang completed in 2017 and located in the Old City district of Beijing. Initially, the original building was a 262 square meter common courtyard house. It has been transformed into five apartments with independent courtyards, as well as a space accessible to public that hosts a cafe and tea house. This project combines old urban renewal, courtyard renovation and a research on ideal house. Indeed, the layout of the «garden house» and the «public unit»  fits into the structure of contemporary society, transforming the courtyard house into a «miniature community.» The design of the apartments in minimal size serves the spiritual construction of the «garden house harmonization», and transforms the experience of everyday poetry and urban landscape into the «ideal living environment» through the narrative of space. This project also provides an extension of public space from the street and completes the established «street + residential unit» model, transforming the courtyard into a «miniature community». This collective space can be used and shared by all residents of the unit on a daily basis, and can be opened to neighbouring hutongs and foreign visitors. This space then becomes a place of public service shared by a larger number of neighbors and reinforces its «community» character.The interview is especially based on the analysis of the ‘Miniature Beijing’ project : a conversion of No. 28 Dayuan Hutong Beijing in collective housing, sharing spaces and facilities#China #contemporarychinesearchitecture #density #housing #architecture #cag #atelierli #lixinggang #architectureinterviews #architectinterviews #lifestyle #collectivehousing #minimalliving #insideoutside #massproduction #customedarchitecture #context #hutong #history

After a careful study of this process, we created a specific architectural scenography that gives people a singular sensory experience of the making of traditional Chinese liquor. 

Seeds are the main raw material used to make Chinese liquor. At the entrance lobby, various seeds are placed in Plexiglas tubes to create a vibrant screen with a huge pattern.

Shuifa Geographic Information Industrial Park Exhibition Center 
#Jinan, #China

The project is located in the Changqing Economic Development Zone, 20 kilometers away from the city centre of Jinan. In order to give visitors the best viewing experience, the designer has isolated the area from the surrounding environment and has created a relatively enclosed space.

The building’s main functions are hosting residential sales expos, property expos, and offices. The main entrance is located on the west side. In order to eliminate the visual impact of the messy surrounding environment, geometrical hills are designed to surround the square, which slowly rises as people enter the site, gradually blocking out the view. Mountains, water, and marble are fused together in this undeveloped wilderness.

A second layer is set outside the main structure - perforated plating, so that the building is enveloped within the perforated plating, forming a relatively enclosed space. The curtain wall sections are slanted, nestled, and interlaced inside, and the gap between the sections naturally forms the entrance of the building. Everything happens inside the space covered by the perforated plate curtain wall, connected to the outside world only through the irregular gaps. The interior of the building is obscured by the white perforated plating, and as night falls, light shines through the perforated plates to make the whole building glow, like a piece of shiny marble standing in the wilderness.

PRODUCTION*Density / Ecological Urbanism (Taillandier Paris)Curator : Marine Fritsch Master 1 @ensa_versailles The project of No. 28 Dayuan Hu Tong, titled «Miniature Beijing», is a transformation project by Atelier Li Xinggang completed in 2017 and located in the Old City district of Beijing. Initially, the original building was a 262 square meter common courtyard house. It has been transformed into five apartments with independent courtyards, as well as a space accessible to public that hosts a cafe and tea house. This project combines old urban renewal, courtyard renovation and a research on ideal house. Indeed, the layout of the «garden house» and the «public unit»  fits into the structure of contemporary society, transforming the courtyard house into a «miniature community.» The design of the apartments in minimal size serves the spiritual construction of the «garden house harmonization», and transforms the experience of everyday poetry and urban landscape into the «ideal living environment» through the narrative of space. This project also provides an extension of public space from the street and completes the established «street + residential unit» model, transforming the courtyard into a «miniature community». This collective space can be used and shared by all residents of the unit on a daily basis, and can be opened to neighbouring hutongs and foreign visitors. This space then becomes a place of public service shared by a larger number of neighbors and reinforces its «community» character.The interview is especially based on the analysis of the ‘Miniature Beijing’ project : a conversion of No. 28 Dayuan Hutong Beijing in collective housing, sharing spaces and facilities

He is the founder of Run atelier dedicated to 3 domains : general projects, teaching and the last one is focusing on «reshaping the value of places». One of his goals is to lead the traditional Chinese archi- tecture in a contemporary way. Within his teaching career he founded the Construction Society, an academic group that focused on residential wood architecture and craftsmanship. For him as an architect : exploring and researching materials are fundamentals.The interview is especially based on the analysis of the Guiyuan New Village Community Renovation Yuecheng in Zhejiang province 2018

PRODUCTION*Density / Ecological Urbanism (Taillandier Paris)Curator : @laura_cbf Laura Chambefort Master 1 ENSA VersaillesIn 2016 @peoplesarchitecture offers their first plugin house. With their experience after setting up their office in the heart of the Hutong of Beijing. The agency questions the possible rehabilitation of historical districts of the Chinese capital.The Hutong are the historical urban system of Beijing, characterized by the tangle of alleys and courtyards, the buildings are arranged in a  fine and very dense mesh.Some of them are more than 700 years old, and the population of these historic districts was abandoned by their inhabitants who preferred to move to the Beijing suburbs with more modern housing. Thus the Hutong, the historical heart of the capital, became a slum. It is in this context that Mrs Fan, the inhabitant of the plugin house realized by PAO, grew up. When she was young, her parents originally from Hutong chose to move to the suburbs. Mrs. Fan, once married and an adult, decided to become independent. Faced with their precarious real estate situation and a rethinking of their way of living, the Fan couple decided to turn to the Hutong. (…)The interview is especially based on the analysis of 2 plugin houses:Shenzen's Shangwei Village, province du Guangdong South China, 2018Mrs Fan's house Historic Beijing Hutong, 2016

Welcome to a special journey through the traditional making of Chinese liquor! A glimpse at our newly completed project :Chinese liquor themed boutique hotel.

For this renovation project, the client wanted the new design to focus on the topic of traditional Chinese liquor. In China, alcohol is made from cereal seeds, following a traditional liquor-making process that has been used over centuries. 

After a careful study of this process, we created a specific architectural scenography that gives people a singular sensory experience of the making of traditional Chinese liquor. 

"Jiu Qu", a brick shaped solid composite of yeast and mold, is used for saccharification and fermentation. We used these vegetal bricks to create the counter of the bar, which gives an olfactive experience to the user. The countertop is made of custom terrazzo fabricated on site with pieces of green glass from local bottles of liquor.

I learned from @colleudumond (merci!) that the garden I shared yesterday at Chaumont-sur-Loire was designed by Wang Shu, a Chinese architect who has won the Pritzker prize. I looked up more of his work and was very interested in much of what I saw and read. Both in terms of how he and several other architects have been changing Chinese architecture in the last 20 or so years, but also in the specifics of how. Particularly interesting to me was Wang Shu’s Ningbo History Museum where he used materials salvaged from building and villages that had been cleared for the project in the facade. In his own words the design was a kind of resistance against the thoughtfulness destruction of their history. This was designed in 2008 around the same time as the Beijing Olympics, so I can only imagine how relevant that statement was.

Interesting to me is that I recognize a global trend that we also saw in Europe and elsewhere in the same period using salvaged and traditional materials in a way that honored but also transcends the vernacular.

The museum intentionally reminds us of both large ruins and fortresses and is an imposing figure in the landscape. The angles of the facade create tension and different scale spaces from very large to intimate, and paths seem to zigzag between. The contrast of the deeply textural and detailed facade to the enormous scale of the building adds so much. It is the materials that bring the whole building to life for me and make it most interesting.

#Jinan, #China

The project is located in the Changqing Economic Development Zone, 20 kilometers away from the city centre of Jinan. In order to give visitors the best viewing experience, the designer has isolated the area from the surrounding environment and has created a relatively enclosed space.

The building’s main functions are hosting residential sales expos, property expos, and offices. The main entrance is located on the west side. In order to eliminate the visual impact of the messy surrounding environment, geometrical hills are designed to surround the square, which slowly rises as people enter the site, gradually blocking out the view. Mountains, water, and marble are fused together in this undeveloped wilderness.

A second layer is set outside the main structure - perforated plating, so that the building is enveloped within the perforated plating, forming a relatively enclosed space. The curtain wall sections are slanted, nestled, and interlaced inside, and the gap between the sections naturally forms the entrance of the building. Everything happens inside the space covered by the perforated plate curtain wall, connected to the outside world only through the irregular gaps. The interior of the building is obscured by the white perforated plating, and as night falls, light shines through the perforated plates to make the whole building glow, like a piece of shiny marble standing in the wilderness.

description: PRODUCTION*Density / Ecological Urbanism (Taillandier Paris)Curator : Marine Fritsch Master 1 @ensa_versailles The project of No. 28 Dayuan Hu Tong, titled «Miniature Beijing», is a transformation project by Atelier Li Xinggang completed in 2017 and located in the Old City district of Beijing. Initially, the original building was a 262 square meter common courtyard house. It has been transformed into five apartments with independent courtyards, as well as a space accessible to public that hosts a cafe and tea house. This project combines old urban renewal, courtyard renovation and a research on ideal house. Indeed, the layout of the «garden house» and the «public unit»  fits into the structure of contemporary society, transforming the courtyard house into a «miniature community.» The design of the apartments in minimal size serves the spiritual construction of the «garden house harmonization», and transforms the experience of everyday poetry and urban landscape into the «ideal living environment» through the narrative of space. This project also provides an extension of public space from the street and completes the established «street + residential unit» model, transforming the courtyard into a «miniature community». This collective space can be used and shared by all residents of the unit on a daily basis, and can be opened to neighbouring hutongs and foreign visitors. This space then becomes a place of public service shared by a larger number of neighbors and reinforces its «community» character.The interview is especially based on the analysis of the ‘Miniature Beijing’ project : a conversion of No. 28 Dayuan Hutong Beijing in collective housing, sharing spaces and facilities#China #contemporarychinesearchitecture #density #housing #architecture #cag #atelierli #lixinggang #architectureinterviews #architectinterviews #lifestyle #collectivehousing #minimalliving #insideoutside #massproduction #customedarchitecture #context #hutong #history

I learned from @colleudumond (merci!) that the garden I shared yesterday at Chaumont-sur-Loire was designed by Wang Shu, a Chinese architect who has won the Pritzker prize. I looked up more of his work and was very interested in much of what I saw and read. Both in terms of how he and several other architects have been changing Chinese architecture in the last 20 or so years, but also in the specifics of how. Particularly interesting to me was Wang Shu’s Ningbo History Museum where he used materials salvaged from building and villages that had been cleared for the project in the facade. In his own words the design was a kind of resistance against the thoughtfulness destruction of their history. This was designed in 2008 around the same time as the Beijing Olympics, so I can only imagine how relevant that statement was.

Interesting to me is that I recognize a global trend that we also saw in Europe and elsewhere in the same period using salvaged and traditional materials in a way that honored but also transcends the vernacular.

The museum intentionally reminds us of both large ruins and fortresses and is an imposing figure in the landscape. The angles of the facade create tension and different scale spaces from very large to intimate, and paths seem to zigzag between. The contrast of the deeply textural and detailed facade to the enormous scale of the building adds so much. It is the materials that bring the whole building to life for me and make it most interesting.

La restauración de este patrimonio industrial es una sutil reinterpretación de la “Era Roja” de China. Este edificio de los años 70 solía ser el comedor de los trabajadores de las minas de carbón. Se encuentra junto a lo que solían ser los edificios de oficinas de la mina de carbón, que fueron construidos en 1912 por arquitectos alemanes, y presenta las características típicas de la arquitectura occidental en China de la época, con un uso intensivo de elementos de arco.

河北邯郸 Handan , Hebei Province

In front of the Xiangtangshan Grottoes(响堂山石窟), there used to be Chang‘le Temple. In a fire in 1947, most of the above-ground structures were destroyed. The only structures remaining are an octagonal nine-story Louge-Style (楼阁式) Song Dynasty pagoda, known as the Putong Pagoda (普同塔), two Song Dynasty scripture pillars(经幢) and over a dozen stone steles from various historical periods.

定林寺 | Dinglin Temple
山西晋城 Jincheng, Shanxi Province

The age of Dinglin Temple is unknown, and it has undergone repairs during various dynasties, blending multiple architectural styles from the Jin, Yuan, Ming, and Qing periods. The existing mountain gate, Leiying Hall(雷音殿), and the eastern and western side halls are structures from the Yuan Dynasty. The mountain gate has a width of three bays, a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof(重檐歇山顶), with a brick lower level and a wooden upper level. The Leiying Hall has a square floor plan with exquisite bracket sets, and its decorative roof ridges are excellent examples of Jin Dynasty glazed tile craftsmanship.

草庵寺 | Cao’an Temple
福建泉州 Quanzhou, Fujian Province

The only surviving Manichaeism(摩尼教) temple in China, Cao’an Temple, originated in the Song Dynasty as a simple grass structure. In the Yuan Dynasty (1339 AD), it was transformed into a stone-structured hip-and gable(歇山式) style building, built against a cliff, exhibiting simplicity and antiquity. It serves as a valuable material basis for studying ancient maritime communication between ancient China and Persia.

崔府君庙 | Cuifujun Temple
山西晋城 Jincheng, Shanxi Province

Cuifujun Temple is the only existing Han-Tang platform-style(高台式) architecture in China, with high historical value. The entire temple consists of over 50 halls, all built with brick and wood structures. The mountain gate is the oldest, dating back to the Jin Dynasty. It is situated on a high platform, featuring a double-eaved, hip-and-gable roof(重檐歇山顶). The roof is adorned with colored copper tiles, displaying colorful patterns.

玄帝庙 | Xuandi Temple
山西运城 Yuncheng, Shanxi Province

Xuandi Temple is completed in the Ming Dynasty (1603), it is a Taoist temple dedicated to the worship of Emperor Xuanwu. The overall layout of the temple is solemn, and the architectural hierarchy is clear. Along the central axis, from south to north, there are four buildings in sequence: mountain gate, incense pavilion, main hall, and Shengong Shengmu Temple (temple dedicated to the Holy Father and Holy Mother). It is a typical example of Ming Dynasty architecture. The most distinctive feature of the temple is that all the roofs of the buildings are covered with glazed tiles.

双龙桥 | Shuanglong Bridge
云南红河哈尼族彝族自治州 Honghe Hani and Yi Autonomous Prefecture, Yunnan Province

Shuanglong Bridge was initially constructed during the Ming Dynasty and underwent restoration in the Qing Dynasty. The bridge features seventeen arches, and its structure consists of approximately 500 large, meticulously chiseled stone blocks, with stone parapets lining both sides. The central pavilion of the bridge stands out with its elaborately crafted, high-pitched eaves and is renowned as the 'Grand Pavilion of Southern Yunnan’(滇南大观楼).

宏村 | Hongcun Ancient Village
安徽黄山 Huangshan, Anhui Province

Hongcun boasts a wealth of historical buildings from the Ming and Qing periods. The village is also equipped with a well-designed water system, featuring meandering waterways that provide domestic water for each household. This is a typical representation of Huizhou residential architecture. The buildings primarily include residences and private gardens, along with public facilities such as academies and ancestral halls, forming a relatively complete architectural ensemble. Various structures emphasize intricate decorations, including delicate and exquisite woodcarvings, brick carvings, and stone carvings, possessing extremely high artistic value.

南樊石牌坊 | Nanfan Stone Archway
山西运城 Yuncheng, Shanxi Province

Nanfan Stone Archway is a filial piety arch built in the Qing Dynasty (1804). The arch is made of stone with a structure imitating wood. From the base to the top, it is adorned with various forms of stone carvings, including animals, flowers, and figures. There are round-carved stone lions on the arch posts. A stele pavilion is to the right of the arch, with excellent calligraphy and carving, well-preserved.

Seeing Traditional Chinese Feng Shui through Traditional Chinese Architecture 
with Jun (E1) 

The traditional Chinese architecture tend to rely on ornaments with auspicious implications for the impressive effect. The ornaments can be inspired by legends, myths or Chinese folk customs etc.

For example, this historical house has a total of 12 swallow tails located neatly on the ridges. Legend has it that in ancient China, it is believed that humans need the blessings of heaven and earth to survive, therefore they respect heaven greatly. The bird on the roof is like an angel – a spiritual creature that can reach heaven and worship Gods. “12” is believed to be an auspicious number.

Feng Shui implementation varies from different cultures and different personal tastes. It is not 
tied to any styles and certainly not to any objects. In order to truly understand the essence of Feng Shui and practice it well, you first must have pretty good understanding of the culture in which Feng Shui originated. You could then use it as a tool to integrate into your own living environment, not just blindly follow the principles.

description:
独乐寺 | Dule Temple
天津 Tianjin

The oldest existing structures in Dule Temple are the Mountain Gate and Guanyin Pavilion（观音阁）, both rebuilt during the Liao Dynasty in 984. The Guanyin Pavilion is the oldest existing wooden pavilion structure(楼阁) in China, constructed to protect the giant statue of Guanyin inside. Its design combines the robustness of the Tang Dynasty with the gracefulness of the Song Dynasty. It is a three-story wooden pavilion with a hidden second floor. Externally, it appears as a two-story structure, with a width of five bays and a depth of four bays. The construction utilized 24 different types of brackets(斗拱) without the use of any nails. Despite experiencing multiple earthquakes throughout history, it still stands tall, making it a marvel in architectural history.

三倒拐 | Sandaoguai
重庆 Chongqing

Sandaoguai is a complex of Ming and Qing Dynasty street-market architecture. The entire street surface is paved with bluestones. It alternates between steep and gentle, winding forward in a meandering manner. The buildings in Sandaoguai predominantly feature the Chuangdou structure(穿斗式), supplemented by Tailiang structures(抬梁式). They mostly take the form of Ming and Qing quadrangle courtyards, with small blue-tiled roofs. The roofs are a combination of overhanging-gable(悬山) and hip-and-gable(歇山) styles, presenting a simple and elegant charm.

凤斌堂 | Fengbin Hall
福建泉州 Quanzhou, Fujian Province

Fengbin Hall is divided into upper and lower levels, each built on platforms made of stacked boulders. This wooden building adopts a suspended structure(吊脚楼), hanging approximately 1 meter above the ground. Interestingly, from the front, it appears as a two-story wooden building; from the side, the upper and lower levels appear relatively independent. The interiors of the upper and lower levels are also not connected, accessible only by external stairs.

北京園博園，坐落於偶豐台區永定河邊，曾是第九屆中國國際園林博覽會的舉辦地，如今是一座集園林藝術、文化景觀、生態休閑、科普教育於一體的大型公益性城市公園。
園博園以「一軸、兩點、五園」為設計布局，園中建築兼具現代和古典風情，古色古香的園林風景吸引不少漢服愛好者前去打卡。

霍州观音庙 | Huozhou Guanyin Temple
山西临汾 Linfen, Shanxi Province

Huozhou Guanyin Temple is a temple complex that integrates Confucianism, Buddhism, and Taoism. It is a square-shaped temple with two parallel axes. There are currently eight halls from different dynasties, including the Song, Yuan, Ming, and Qing periods. The Yuan Dynasty cross-street pavilion has an wood structure with a columned corridor at the bottom serving as a cross-street passage. The roof is covered with gray tiles, outlined with with glazed ceramic tile.

玄帝庙 | Xuandi Temple
山西运城 Yuncheng, Shanxi Province

Xuandi Temple is completed in the Ming Dynasty (1603), it is a Taoist temple dedicated to the worship of Emperor Xuanwu. The overall layout of the temple is solemn, and the architectural hierarchy is clear. Along the central axis, from south to north, there are four buildings in sequence: mountain gate, incense pavilion, main hall, and Shengong Shengmu Temple (temple dedicated to the Holy Father and Holy Mother). It is a typical example of Ming Dynasty architecture. The most distinctive feature of the temple is that all the roofs of the buildings are covered with glazed tiles.

The design is exquisite, with subtle and ingenious details, surpassing all others in its class, making it a unique national treasure.

胡氏古民居 | Hu Family Ancient Residence
甘肃天水 Tianshui , Gansu Province

The Hu Family Ancient Residence was constructed during the Ming Dynasty (1608-1615) by an official Hu Laijin and inhabited by its descendants. Due to the dry climate in the northwest region, the ancient brick and wood structures have been well-preserved. They are considered a ”rare group of ancient residential buildings with typical Ming Dynasty architectural styles“ nationwide. The existing buildings are divided into the South Residence and the North Residence, comprising eight buildings with a total of twenty-six rooms. The architectural layout, structural design, roof ridge decorations, brick and wood carvings, and more possess high historical, artistic, and scientific value.

黄姚古镇 | Huangyao Ancient Town
广西贺州 Hezhou, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region

Huangyao Ancient Town originated during the Song Dynasty and has a history of nearly 1000 years. Flourishing at one time due to convenient waterways, it preserves over 20 temples and shrines, as well as more than 10 pavilions and towers, predominantly built during the Ming and Qing dynasties. Jiayuguan, built in 1372 during the Ming Dynasty, is the first major pass at the western end of the Ming Great Wall and a crucial junction on the ancient Silk Road. 三倒拐 | Sandaoguai
重庆 Chongqing

Sandaoguai is a complex of Ming and Qing Dynasty street-market architecture. The entire street surface is paved with bluestones. The buildings in Sandaoguai predominantly feature the Chuangdou structure(穿斗式), supplemented by Tailiang structures(抬梁式). They mostly take the form of Ming and Qing quadrangle courtyards, with small blue-tiled roofs. The roofs are a combination of overhanging-gable(悬山) and hip-and-gable(歇山) styles, presenting a simple and elegant charm.

云南红河哈尼族彝族自治州 Honghe Hani and Yi Autonomous Prefecture, Yunnan Province

Shuanglong Bridge was initially constructed during the Ming Dynasty and underwent restoration in the Qing Dynasty. The bridge features seventeen arches, and its structure consists of approximately 500 large, meticulously chiseled stone blocks, with stone parapets lining both sides. The central pavilion of the bridge stands out with its elaborately crafted, high-pitched eaves and is renowned as the 'Grand Pavilion of Southern Yunnan’(滇南大观楼).

福建泉州 Quanzhou, Fujian Province

The only surviving Manichaeism(摩尼教) temple in China, Cao’an Temple, originated in the Song Dynasty as a simple grass structure. In the Yuan Dynasty (1339 AD), it was transformed into a stone-structured hip-and gable(歇山式) style building, built against a cliff, exhibiting simplicity and antiquity. It serves as a valuable material basis for studying ancient maritime communication between ancient China and Persia.

独乐寺 | Dule Temple
天津 Tianjin

The oldest existing structures in Dule Temple are the Mountain Gate and Guanyin Pavilion（观音阁）, both rebuilt during the Liao Dynasty in 984. The Guanyin Pavilion is the oldest existing wooden pavilion structure(楼阁) in China, constructed to protect the giant statue of Guanyin inside. Its design combines the robustness of the Tang Dynasty with the gracefulness of the Song Dynasty. It is a three-story wooden pavilion with a hidden second floor. Externally, it appears as a two-story structure, with a width of five bays and a depth of four bays. The construction utilized 24 different types of brackets(斗拱) without the use of any nails. Despite experiencing multiple earthquakes throughout history, it still stands tall, making it a marvel in architectural history.

大三巴牌坊 | Ruins of St. Paul's
澳门 Macau

This is the ruin of the façade of the St. Paul's Church in Macau. The original church was built in 1603 during the Portuguese occupation of Macau, making it the first Baroque-style architecture in China. Decorative elements from the East, such as traditional Chinese-style stone lions, were integrated with classical European elements. In 1835, a fire burned down the church, leaving only the façade, some foundations, and the stone steps in front of the church.

独乐寺 | Dule Temple
天津 Tianjin

The oldest existing structures in Dule Temple are the Mountain Gate and Guanyin Pavilion（观音阁）, both rebuilt during the Liao Dynasty in 984. The Guanyin Pavilion is the oldest existing wooden pavilion structure(楼阁) in China, constructed to protect the giant statue of Guanyin inside. Its design combines the robustness of the Tang Dynasty with the gracefulness of the Song Dynasty. It is a three-story wooden pavilion with a hidden second floor. Externally, it appears as a two-story structure, with a width of five bays and a depth of four bays. The construction utilized 24 different types of brackets(斗拱) without the use of any nails. Despite experiencing multiple earthquakes throughout history, it still stands tall, making it a marvel in architectural history.

This is the ruin of the façade of the St. Paul's Church in Macau. 独乐寺 | Dule Temple

The oldest existing structures in Dule Temple are the Mountain Gate and Guanyin Pavilion（观音阁）, both rebuilt during the Liao Dynasty in 984. The Guanyin Pavilion is the oldest existing wooden pavilion structure(楼阁) in China, constructed to protect the giant statue of Guanyin inside. Its design combines the robustness of the Tang Dynasty with the gracefulness of the Song Dynasty. It is a three-story wooden pavilion with a hidden second floor. Externally, it appears as a two-story structure, with a width of five bays and a depth of four bays. The construction utilized 24 different types of brackets(斗拱) without the use of any nails. Despite experiencing multiple earthquakes throughout history, it still stands tall, making it a marvel in architectural history.

What we did in Chiang Mai on 24 October! 

1. Lanterns are being hung all over the city, including at the Wat Phra Singh. The festival is celebrated on the night of the full moon in the 12th lunar month, which this year falls in November. It’s a shame we won’t be here to experience this magical, romantic and enchanting sight 🏮🌌

2. This is the Three Kings Monument. It shows the three founding fathers of Chiang Mai- King Mengrai, King Ramkhamhaeng and King Ngam Muang 👑🤴👑

3. The entrance to the prayer hall at Wat Dok Euang is so richly decorated. Through the front door you can just about see the golden Buddhas at the main altar ☸️

4. Inside there are lovely murals showing stories of Buddha 🪷

5. We walked all the way to the Ping River which runs through Chiang Mai outside the old city. There were a few hotels, bars and restaurants we saw on the opposite river bank. The Ping river is one of the prime viewing spots during the Yi Peng Lantern Festival to see the lanterns in the sky and floating floral offerings 🏞️

6. The Pung Tao Gong ancestral temple was founded in 1876, but the shrine fell into ruin as the city's Chinese population declined. It was rebuilt during the city’s 700th anniversary celebrations 🇨🇳

7. This is the inside of the new temple, which follows traditional Chinese architecture 🐉

8. The unsuspecting monk in the grounds of Wat Upakhut is in danger of having his head bitten off by the tiger! 🐅

9. Found a number of chickens roaming around Wat Saen Fang. They’re so fluffy it looks like they have trousers on… 🐓

10. Who says money can’t buy you happiness… 🤑

独乐寺 | Dule Temple
天津 Tianjin

The oldest existing structures in Dule Temple are the Mountain Gate and Guanyin Pavilion（观音阁）, both rebuilt during the Liao Dynasty in 984. The Guanyin Pavilion is the oldest existing wooden pavilion structure(楼阁) in China, constructed to protect the giant statue of Guanyin inside. Its design combines the robustness of the Tang Dynasty with the gracefulness of the Song Dynasty. It is a three-story wooden pavilion with a hidden second floor. Externally, it appears as a two-story structure, with a width of five bays and a depth of four bays. The construction utilized 24 different types of brackets(斗拱) without the use of any nails. Despite experiencing multiple earthquakes throughout history, it still stands tall, making it a marvel in architectural history.

What we did in Chiang Mai on 24 October! 

1. Lanterns are being hung all over the city, including at the Wat Phra Singh. The Yi Peng Lantern Festival in Chiang Mai is famous for the sight of thousands of lit lanterns made of paper rising into the night sky. The festival is celebrated on the night of the full moon in the 12th lunar month, which this year falls in November. It’s a shame we won’t be here to experience this magical, romantic and enchanting sight 🏮🌌

2. This is the Three Kings Monument. It shows the three founding fathers of Chiang Mai- King Mengrai, King Ramkhamhaeng and King Ngam Muang 👑🤴👑

3. The entrance to the prayer hall at Wat Dok Euang is so richly decorated. Through the front door you can just about see the golden Buddhas at the main altar ☸️

4. Inside there are lovely murals showing stories of Buddha 🪷

5. We walked all the way to the Ping River which runs through Chiang Mai outside the old city. There were a few hotels, bars and restaurants we saw on the opposite river bank. The Ping river is one of the prime viewing spots during the Yi Peng Lantern Festival to see the lanterns in the sky and floating floral offerings 🏞️

6. The Pung Tao Gong ancestral temple was founded in 1876, but the shrine fell into ruin as the city's Chinese population declined. It was rebuilt during the city’s 700th anniversary celebrations 🇨🇳

7. This is the inside of the new temple, which follows traditional Chinese architecture 🐉

8. The unsuspecting monk in the grounds of Wat Upakhut is in danger of having his head bitten off by the tiger! 🐅

9. Found a number of chickens roaming around Wat Saen Fang. They’re so fluffy it looks like they have trousers on… 🐓

10. Who says money can’t buy you happiness… 🤑

What we did in Chiang Mai on 24 October! 

1. Lanterns are being hung all over the city, including at the Wat Phra Singh. The Yi Peng Lantern Festival in Chiang Mai is famous for the sight of thousands of lit lanterns made of paper rising into the night sky. The festival is celebrated on the night of the full moon in the 12th lunar month, which this year falls in November. It’s a shame we won’t be here to experience this magical, romantic and enchanting sight 🏮🌌

2. This is the Three Kings Monument. It shows the three founding fathers of Chiang Mai- King Mengrai, King Ramkhamhaeng and King Ngam Muang 👑🤴👑

3. The entrance to the prayer hall at Wat Dok Euang is so richly decorated. Through the front door you can just about see the golden Buddhas at the main altar ☸️

4. Inside there are lovely murals showing stories of Buddha 🪷

5. We walked all the way to the Ping River which runs through Chiang Mai outside the old city. There were a few hotels, bars and restaurants we saw on the opposite river bank. The Ping river is one of the prime viewing spots during the Yi Peng Lantern Festival to see the lanterns in the sky and floating floral offerings 🏞️

6. The Pung Tao Gong ancestral temple was founded in 1876, but the shrine fell into ruin as the city's Chinese population declined. It was rebuilt during the city’s 700th anniversary celebrations 🇨🇳

7. This is the inside of the new temple, which follows traditional Chinese architecture 🐉

8. The unsuspecting monk in the grounds of Wat Upakhut is in danger of having his head bitten off by the tiger! 🐅

9. Found a number of chickens roaming around Wat Saen Fang. They’re so fluffy it looks like they have trousers on… 🐓

云南红河哈尼族彝族自治州 Honghe Hani and Yi Autonomous Prefecture, Yunnan Province

Shuanglong Bridge was initially constructed during the Ming Dynasty and underwent restoration in the Qing Dynasty. 三倒拐 | Sandaoguai
重庆 Chongqing

Sandaoguai is a complex of Ming and Qing Dynasty street-market architecture. The entire street surface is paved with bluestones. It alternates between steep and gentle, winding forward in a meandering manner. The buildings in Sandaoguai predominantly feature the Chuangdou structure(穿斗式), supplemented by Tailiang structures(抬梁式). They mostly take the form of Ming and Qing quadrangle courtyards, with small blue-tiled roofs. The roofs are a combination of overhanging-gable(悬山) and hip-and-gable(歇山) styles, presenting a simple and elegant charm.

Its brick carvings, wood carvings, and other detailed decorations hold significant artistic value.

Jiayuguan, built in 1372 during the Ming Dynasty, is the first major pass at the western end of the Ming Great Wall and a crucial junction on the ancient Silk Road. 【#遊山玩水】雪中如琴湖 Ruqin Lake in Lushan, Jiangxi
如琴湖，是廬山其中一處風景名勝，因湖面形狀猶如小提琴，故而得名。
小雪時分，如琴湖四周被皚皚白雪覆蓋着，銀裝白雪，水平如鏡，與湖中的亭榭曲橋相映成趣，仿佛來到了童話中的雪國仙境。
唐朝著名詩人白居易，亦曾到訪如琴湖賞花，「人間四月芳菲盡，山寺桃花始盛開」所寫的正是此地。

云南红河哈尼族彝族自治州 Honghe Hani and Yi Autonomous Prefecture, Yunnan Province

Shuanglong Bridge was initially constructed during the Ming Dynasty and underwent restoration in the Qing Dynasty. The bridge features seventeen arches, and its structure consists of approximately 500 large, meticulously chiseled stone blocks, with stone parapets lining both sides. The central pavilion of the bridge stands out with its elaborately crafted, high-pitched eaves and is renowned as the 'Grand Pavilion of Southern Yunnan’(滇南大观楼).

定林寺 | Dinglin Temple
山西晋城 Jincheng, Shanxi Province

The age of Dinglin Temple is unknown, and it has undergone repairs during various dynasties, blending multiple architectural styles from the Jin, Yuan, Ming, and Qing periods. The existing mountain gate, Leiying Hall(雷音殿), and the eastern and western side halls are structures from the Yuan Dynasty. The mountain gate has a width of three bays, a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof(重檐歇山顶), with a brick lower level and a wooden upper level. The Leiying Hall has a square floor plan with exquisite bracket sets, and its decorative roof ridges are excellent examples of Jin Dynasty glazed tile craftsmanship.

Kaibao Temple Glazed Tile Pagoda is a 13-story octagonal Louge-style(楼阁式) tower. The tower is adorned with red, brown, blue, and green glazed bricks. 世德堂 | Shide Hall
浙江金华 Jinhua , Zhejiang Province

Shide Hall was built to worship two generals from the Southern Song Dynasty. It features a flush-gable roof, a layout with three courtyards, and is composed of elements such as a screen wall, front hall (gatehouse, stage), front courtyard, two front corridors, middle hall, rear courtyard, two rear corridors, and rear hall. Shide Hall is an important tangible example for the study of the architectural form and traditional building craftsmanship of ancestral halls in Zhejiang. Its brick carvings, wood carvings, and other detailed decorations hold significant artistic value.

胡氏古民居 | Hu Family Ancient Residence
甘肃天水 Tianshui , Gansu Province

The Hu Family Ancient Residence was constructed during the Ming Dynasty (1608-1615) by an official Hu Laijin and inhabited by its descendants. Due to the dry climate in the northwest region, the ancient brick and wood structures have been well-preserved. They are considered a ”rare group of ancient residential buildings with typical Ming Dynasty architectural styles“ nationwide. The existing buildings are divided into the South Residence and the North Residence, comprising eight buildings with a total of twenty-six rooms. The architectural layout, structural design, roof ridge decorations, brick and wood carvings, and more possess high historical, artistic, and scientific value.

The layout of the buildings centers around the Tianhou Hall(天后殿), which serves as the main place of worship, extending from north to south. What we did in Chiang Mai on 24 October! 

1. Lanterns are being hung all over the city, including at the Wat Phra Singh. The Yi Peng Lantern Festival in Chiang Mai is famous for the sight of thousands of lit lanterns made of paper rising into the night sky. The festival is celebrated on the night of the full moon in the 12th lunar month, which this year falls in November. It’s a shame we won’t be here to experience this magical, romantic and enchanting sight 🏮🌌

2. This is the Three Kings Monument. It shows the three founding fathers of Chiang Mai- King Mengrai, King Ramkhamhaeng and King Ngam Muang 👑🤴👑

3. The entrance to the prayer hall at Wat Dok Euang is so richly decorated. Through the front door you can just about see the golden Buddhas at the main altar ☸️

4. Inside there are lovely murals showing stories of Buddha 🪷

5. We walked all the way to the Ping River which runs through Chiang Mai outside the old city. There were a few hotels, bars and restaurants we saw on the opposite river bank. The Ping river is one of the prime viewing spots during the Yi Peng Lantern Festival to see the lanterns in the sky and floating floral offerings 🏞️

6. The Pung Tao Gong ancestral temple was founded in 1876, but the shrine fell into ruin as the city's Chinese population declined. It was rebuilt during the city’s 700th anniversary celebrations 🇨🇳

7. This is the inside of the new temple, which follows traditional Chinese architecture 🐉

8. The unsuspecting monk in the grounds of Wat Upakhut is in danger of having his head bitten off by the tiger! 🐅

9. Found a number of chickens roaming around Wat Saen Fang. They’re so fluffy it looks like they have trousers on… 🐓

10. Who says money can’t buy you happiness… 🤑

镇国塔 | Zhenguo Pagoda
福建泉州 Quanzhou , Fujian Province

Zhenguo Pagoda is located in the Kaiyuan Temple(开元寺) in Quanzhou. Initially, it was a wooden pagoda, but due to disasters, it was later reconstructed as a stone pagoda. This pagoda is a Louge-style(楼阁式) building constructed entirely from granite, designed to mimic wooden structures. The core of the pagoda is robust and sturdy, and the stone carving craftsmanship is exquisite and rustic. It is considered a masterpiece among the stone-built structures of the Song Dynasty in China.

独乐寺 | Dule Temple
天津 Tianjin

The oldest existing structures in Dule Temple are the Mountain Gate and Guanyin Pavilion（观音阁）, both rebuilt during the Liao Dynasty in 984. The Guanyin Pavilion is the oldest existing wooden pavilion structure(楼阁) in China, constructed to protect the giant statue of Guanyin inside. Its design combines the robustness of the Tang Dynasty with the gracefulness of the Song Dynasty. It is a three-story wooden pavilion with a hidden second floor. Externally, it appears as a two-story structure, with a width of five bays and a depth of four bays. The construction utilized 24 different types of brackets(斗拱) without the use of any nails. Despite experiencing multiple earthquakes throughout history, it still stands tall, making it a marvel in architectural history.

What we did in Chiang Mai on 24 October! 

1. Lanterns are being hung all over the city, including at the Wat Phra Singh. The Yi Peng Lantern Festival in Chiang Mai is famous for the sight of thousands of lit lanterns made of paper rising into the night sky. The festival is celebrated on the night of the full moon in the 12th lunar month, which this year falls in November. It’s a shame we won’t be here to experience this magical, romantic and enchanting sight 🏮🌌

2. This is the Three Kings Monument. It shows the three founding fathers of Chiang Mai- King Mengrai, King Ramkhamhaeng and King Ngam Muang 👑🤴👑

3. The entrance to the prayer hall at Wat Dok Euang is so richly decorated. Through the front door you can just about see the golden Buddhas at the main altar ☸️

4. Inside there are lovely murals showing stories of Buddha 🪷

5. We walked all the way to the Ping River which runs through Chiang Mai outside the old city. There were a few hotels, bars and restaurants we saw on the opposite river bank. The Ping river is one of the prime viewing spots during the Yi Peng Lantern Festival to see the lanterns in the sky and floating floral offerings 🏞️

6. The Pung Tao Gong ancestral temple was founded in 1876, but the shrine fell into ruin as the city's Chinese population declined. It was rebuilt during the city’s 700th anniversary celebrations 🇨🇳

7. This is the inside of the new temple, which follows traditional Chinese architecture 🐉

8. The unsuspecting monk in the grounds of Wat Upakhut is in danger of having his head bitten off by the tiger! 🐅

9. Found a number of chickens roaming around Wat Saen Fang. They’re so fluffy it looks like they have trousers on… 🐓

10. Who says money can’t buy you happiness… 🤑

独乐寺 | Dule Temple
天津 Tianjin

The oldest existing structures in Dule Temple are the Mountain Gate and Guanyin Pavilion（观音阁）, both rebuilt during the Liao Dynasty in 984. The Guanyin Pavilion is the oldest existing wooden pavilion structure(楼阁) in China, constructed to protect the giant statue of Guanyin inside. Its design combines the robustness of the Tang Dynasty with the gracefulness of the Song Dynasty. It is a three-story wooden pavilion with a hidden second floor. Externally, it appears as a two-story structure, with a width of five bays and a depth of four bays. The construction utilized 24 different types of brackets(斗拱) without the use of any nails. Despite experiencing multiple earthquakes throughout history, it still stands tall, making it a marvel in architectural history.

三倒拐 | Sandaoguai
重庆 Chongqing

Sandaoguai is a complex of Ming and Qing Dynasty street-market architecture. The entire street surface is paved with bluestones. It alternates between steep and gentle, winding forward in a meandering manner. The buildings in Sandaoguai predominantly feature the Chuangdou structure(穿斗式), supplemented by Tailiang structures(抬梁式). They mostly take the form of Ming and Qing quadrangle courtyards, with small blue-tiled roofs. The roofs are a combination of overhanging-gable(悬山) and hip-and-gable(歇山) styles, presenting a simple and elegant charm.

独乐寺 | Dule Temple
天津 Tianjin

The oldest existing structures in Dule Temple are the Mountain Gate and Guanyin Pavilion（观音阁）, both rebuilt during the Liao Dynasty in 984. The Guanyin Pavilion is the oldest existing wooden pavilion structure(楼阁) in China, constructed to protect the giant statue of Guanyin inside. Its design combines the robustness of the Tang Dynasty with the gracefulness of the Song Dynasty. It is a three-story wooden pavilion with a hidden second floor. Externally, it appears as a two-story structure, with a width of five bays and a depth of four bays. The construction utilized 24 different types of brackets(斗拱) without the use of any nails. Despite experiencing multiple earthquakes throughout history, it still stands tall, making it a marvel in architectural history.

What we did in Chiang Mai on 24 October! 

1. Lanterns are being hung all over the city, including at the Wat Phra Singh. The Yi Peng Lantern Festival in Chiang Mai is famous for the sight of thousands of lit lanterns made of paper rising into the night sky. The festival is celebrated on the night of the full moon in the 12th lunar month, which this year falls in November. It’s a shame we won’t be here to experience this magical, romantic and enchanting sight 🏮🌌

2. This is the Three Kings Monument. It shows the three founding fathers of Chiang Mai- King Mengrai, King Ramkhamhaeng and King Ngam Muang 👑🤴👑

3. The entrance to the prayer hall at Wat Dok Euang is so richly decorated. Through the front door you can just about see the golden Buddhas at the main altar ☸️

4. Inside there are lovely murals showing stories of Buddha 🪷

5. We walked all the way to the Ping River which runs through Chiang Mai outside the old city. There were a few hotels, bars and restaurants we saw on the opposite river bank. The Ping river is one of the prime viewing spots during the Yi Peng Lantern Festival to see the lanterns in the sky and floating floral offerings 🏞️

6. The Pung Tao Gong ancestral temple was founded in 1876, but the shrine fell into ruin as the city's Chinese population declined. It was rebuilt during the city’s 700th anniversary celebrations 🇨🇳

7. This is the inside of the new temple, which follows traditional Chinese architecture 🐉

8. The unsuspecting monk in the grounds of Wat Upakhut is in danger of having his head bitten off by the tiger! 🐅

9. Found a number of chickens roaming around Wat Saen Fang. They’re so fluffy it looks like they have trousers on… 🐓

10. Who says money can’t buy you happiness… 🤑

Seeing Traditional Chinese Feng Shui through Traditional Chinese Architecture 
with Jun (E1) 

The traditional Chinese architecture tend to rely on ornaments with auspicious implications for the impressive effect. The ornaments can be inspired by legends, myths or Chinese folk customs etc.

For example, this historical house has a total of 12 swallow tails located neatly on the ridges. Legend has it that in ancient China, it is believed that humans need the blessings of heaven and earth to survive, therefore they respect heaven greatly. The bird on the roof is like an angel – a spiritual creature that can reach heaven and worship Gods. “12” is believed to be an auspicious number.

Feng Shui implementation varies from different cultures and different personal tastes. It is not 
tied to any styles and certainly not to any objects. In order to truly understand the essence of Feng Shui and practice it well, you first must have pretty good understanding of the culture in which Feng Shui originated. You could then use it as a tool to integrate into your own living environment, not just blindly follow the principles.

Thean Hou Temple, which was Originally built in the Southern Song Dynasty (1196), is the earliest and most grandly structured ancient temple dedicated to Mazu(妈祖). The Tianhou Hall features a multi-eaved, hip-and-gable roof(重檐歇山顶) design, giving the entire structure a tall and majestic appearance, symbolizing the elevated status of Mazu.

What we did in Chiang Mai on 24 October! 

1. Lanterns are being hung all over the city, including at the Wat Phra Singh. The Yi Peng Lantern Festival in Chiang Mai is famous for the sight of thousands of lit lanterns made of paper rising into the night sky. The festival is celebrated on the night of the full moon in the 12th lunar month, which this year falls in November. It’s a shame we won’t be here to experience this magical, romantic and enchanting sight 🏮🌌

2. This is the Three Kings Monument. It shows the three founding fathers of Chiang Mai- King Mengrai, King Ramkhamhaeng and King Ngam Muang 👑🤴👑

3. The entrance to the prayer hall at Wat Dok Euang is so richly decorated. Through the front door you can just about see the golden Buddhas at the main altar ☸️

4. Inside there are lovely murals showing stories of Buddha 🪷

5. We walked all the way to the Ping River which runs through Chiang Mai outside the old city. There were a few hotels, bars and restaurants we saw on the opposite river bank. The Ping river is one of the prime viewing spots during the Yi Peng Lantern Festival to see the lanterns in the sky and floating floral offerings 🏞️

6. The Pung Tao Gong ancestral temple was founded in 1876, but the shrine fell into ruin as the city's Chinese population declined. It was rebuilt during the city’s 700th anniversary celebrations 🇨🇳

7. This is the inside of the new temple, which follows traditional Chinese architecture 🐉

8. The unsuspecting monk in the grounds of Wat Upakhut is in danger of having his head bitten off by the tiger! 🐅

9. Found a number of chickens roaming around Wat Saen Fang. They’re so fluffy it looks like they have trousers on… 🐓

10. Who says money can’t buy you happiness… 🤑

嘉峪关 | Jiayuguan
甘肃嘉峪关 Jiayuguan , Gansu Province

Jiayuguan, built in 1372 during the Ming Dynasty, is the first major pass at the western end of the Ming Great Wall and a crucial junction on the ancient Silk Road. The inner city is the main structure, constructed with rammed earth. The east and west walls have gate openings, each with a barbican entrance(瓮城). Inside the Jiayuguan inner city wall, there are fourteen structures, including arrow towers, enemy towers, corner towers, pavilions, and gate towers, making it one of the most well-preserved among the many gate cities along the Great Wall.

福建泉州 Quanzhou , Fujian Province

Zhenguo Pagoda is located in the Kaiyuan Temple(开元寺) in Quanzhou. Initially, it was a wooden pagoda, but due to disasters, it was later reconstructed as a stone pagoda. The core of the pagoda is robust and sturdy, and the stone carving craftsmanship is exquisite and rustic. It is considered a masterpiece among the stone-built structures of the Song Dynasty in China.

The age of Dinglin Temple is unknown, and it has undergone repairs during various dynasties, blending multiple architectural styles from the Jin, Yuan, Ming, and Qing periods. The existing mountain gate, Leiying Hall(雷音殿), and the eastern and western side halls are structures from the Yuan Dynasty. The Leiying Hall has a square floor plan with exquisite bracket sets, and its decorative roof ridges are excellent examples of Jin Dynasty glazed tile craftsmanship.

镇国塔 | Zhenguo Pagoda
福建泉州 Quanzhou , Fujian Province

Zhenguo Pagoda is located in the Kaiyuan Temple(开元寺) in Quanzhou. Initially, it was a wooden pagoda, but due to disasters, it was later reconstructed as a stone pagoda. This pagoda is a Louge-style(楼阁式) building constructed entirely from granite, designed to mimic wooden structures. The core of the pagoda is robust and sturdy, and the stone carving craftsmanship is exquisite and rustic. It is considered a masterpiece among the stone-built structures of the Song Dynasty in China.

涿鹿县南大寺| South Great Temple in Zhuolu County
河北张家口 Zhangjiakou, Hebei Province

South Great Temple in Zhuolu County currently preserves three remaining structures: the main hall, rear hall, and the west-facing hall. The main hall was built in the Ming Dynasty (year 1480), with a single-eaved hip roof(庑殿顶) and a round-ridge roof(卷棚顶) attatched at the front. The rear hall is a combination of hanging-gable roof(悬山顶) and an attatched round-ridge roof(卷棚顶). After liberation of China, the temple was occupied by a food company for many years, and the halls were converted into warehouses.

山西运城 Yuncheng, Shanxi Province

Nanfan Stone Archway is a filial piety arch built in the Qing Dynasty (1804). The arch is made of stone with a structure imitating wood. From the base to the top, it is adorned with various forms of stone carvings, including animals, flowers, and figures. There are round-carved stone lions on the arch posts. A stele pavilion is to the right of the arch, with excellent calligraphy and carving, well-preserved.

金甲阁 | Jinjia Pavilion
云南玉溪 Yuxi, Yunnan Province

Jinjia Pavilion is located in a village in Yunnan Province, built during the Qing Dynasty in 1838. It is dedicated to Kui Xing(魁星) and consists of three levels. This pavilion has an exquisite design, and at the top, it resembles a brush with thorns inverted into the sky. The internal structure of Jinjia Pavilion is also quite intriguing. The first floor, due to an external corridor, is relatively narrow, so a rare spiral staircase in traditional Chinese architecture is used to save space.

世德堂 | Shide Hall
浙江金华 Jinhua , Zhejiang Province

Shide Hall was built to worship two generals from the Southern Song Dynasty. It features a flush-gable roof, a layout with three courtyards, and is composed of elements such as a screen wall, front hall (gatehouse, stage), front courtyard, two front corridors, middle hall, rear courtyard, two rear corridors, and rear hall. Shide Hall is an important tangible example for the study of the architectural form and traditional building craftsmanship of ancestral halls in Zhejiang. Its brick carvings, wood carvings, and other detailed decorations hold significant artistic value.

天津 Tianjin

Piazza Marco Polo is located in the only ex-Italian concession in contemporary China, established during the Qing Dynasty in 1902. Through an agreement between the Italian envoy and Tianjin, a unique and colorful residential complex of Italian-style garden villas was completed over eight years on Marco Polo Square. The Peace Goddess sculpture, situated at the center of the square, was erected to commemorate the victory of World War I.

The architects selected this concept to reflect traditional Chinese architecture, where courtyards create continuous open spaces. Galaxy SOHO features flowing volumes, connected by bridges, creating a seamless transition between interior and exterior spaces. This design philosophy extends to the distribution of functions across different levels, catering to retail, workspaces, and leisure activities, making it a significant urban landmark in Beijing.

野猪菁桥 | Yezhujing Bridge
云南腾冲 Tengchong, Yunnan Province

Yezhujing Bridge was built in the Qing Dynasty in 1693. During the Sino-Japanese War, it was intentionally destroyed to prevent the Japanese army from advancing. After the victory in the war, it was rebuilt as a cantilevered wooden arch bridge (悬臂式木拱桥). The bridge is constructed by setting piers against the cliffs on both sides, and the main structure is built with five rows of logs layered and compressed according to the lever principle.

开宝寺琉璃塔 | Kaibao Temple Glazed Tile Pagoda
河南开封 Kaifeng, Henan Province

Kaibao Temple Glazed Tile Pagoda is a 13-story octagonal Louge-style(楼阁式) tower. The tower is adorned with red, brown, blue, and green glazed bricks. It is the earliest and tallest extant glazed brick pagoda in China. The tower is embellished with various patterned bricks, featuring over 50 designs such as standing Buddhas, celestial beings, and floral motifs. With its beautiful and lively craftsmanship, it is considered a masterpiece of brick carving art from the Song Dynasty.

双龙桥 | Shuanglong Bridge
云南红河哈尼族彝族自治州 Honghe Hani and Yi Autonomous Prefecture, Yunnan Province

Shuanglong Bridge was initially constructed during the Ming Dynasty and underwent restoration in the Qing Dynasty. The bridge features seventeen arches, and its structure consists of approximately 500 large, meticulously chiseled stone blocks, with stone parapets lining both sides. The central pavilion of the bridge stands out with its elaborately crafted, high-pitched eaves and is renowned as the 'Grand Pavilion of Southern Yunnan’(滇南大观楼).

泉州天后宫 | Thean Hou Temple in Quanzhou
福建泉州 Quanzhou, Fujian Province

Thean Hou Temple, which was Originally built in the Southern Song Dynasty (1196), is the earliest and most grandly structured ancient temple dedicated to Mazu(妈祖). The architectural complex of Tianhou Palace preserves elements from the Song Dynasty and wooden structures from the Ming and Qing Dynasties. The entrance gate is adorned with stone dragon pillars. The layout of the buildings centers around the Tianhou Hall(天后殿), which serves as the main place of worship, extending from north to south. The Tianhou Hall features a multi-eaved, hip-and-gable roof(重檐歇山顶) design, giving the entire structure a tall and majestic appearance, symbolizing the elevated status of Mazu.

What we did in Chiang Mai on 24 October! 

1. Lanterns are being hung all over the city, including at the Wat Phra Singh. The Yi Peng Lantern Festival in Chiang Mai is famous for the sight of thousands of lit lanterns made of paper rising into the night sky. The festival is celebrated on the night of the full moon in the 12th lunar month, which this year falls in November. It’s a shame we won’t be here to experience this magical, romantic and enchanting sight 🏮🌌

2. This is the Three Kings Monument. It shows the three founding fathers of Chiang Mai- King Mengrai, King Ramkhamhaeng and King Ngam Muang 👑🤴👑

3. The entrance to the prayer hall at Wat Dok Euang is so richly decorated. Through the front door you can just about see the golden Buddhas at the main altar ☸️

4. Inside there are lovely murals showing stories of Buddha 🪷

5. We walked all the way to the Ping River which runs through Chiang Mai outside the old city. There were a few hotels, bars and restaurants we saw on the opposite river bank. The Ping river is one of the prime viewing spots during the Yi Peng Lantern Festival to see the lanterns in the sky and floating floral offerings 🏞️

6. The Pung Tao Gong ancestral temple was founded in 1876, but the shrine fell into ruin as the city's Chinese population declined. It was rebuilt during the city’s 700th anniversary celebrations 🇨🇳

云南腾冲 Tengchong, Yunnan Province

Yezhujing Bridge was built in the Qing Dynasty in 1693. During the Sino-Japanese War, it was intentionally destroyed to prevent the Japanese army from advancing. After the victory in the war, it was rebuilt as a cantilevered wooden arch bridge (悬臂式木拱桥). The bridge is constructed by setting piers against the cliffs on both sides, and the main structure is built with five rows of logs layered and compressed according to the lever principle.

Thean Hou Temple, which was Originally built in the Southern Song Dynasty (1196), is the earliest and most grandly structured ancient temple dedicated to Mazu(妈祖). 「平湖秋月」的景觀除了西湖和月亮，還有清代的「一院一樓一碑一亭」的院落布局，與西子湖畔相映成趣，別具韻味。

净土寺 | Jingtu Temple
山西朔州 Shuozhou, Shanxi Province

Jingtu Temple was originally built in the Jin Dynasty (1124), with only the Great Hall and the West Annex Hall remaining. Inside the Great Hall, the ceiling caisson(天花藻井) “celestial palace(天宫楼阁)” is a classic masterpiece of small wooden architecture. The ceiling of this hall is adorned with three caissons(藻井) spanning the entire ceiling, all intricately carved from wood. The design is exquisite, with subtle and ingenious details, surpassing all others in its class, making it a unique national treasure.

【#遊山玩水】天津瓷房子 The Porcelain House, Tianjin
位於天津市赤峰道的瓷房子，曾是法租界的一部分，這棟造型獨特的瓷器房子前身是一棟法式老洋樓，擁有歐式公館的建築結構，如今搖身一變成為了一座「古瓷博物館」。
瓷房子共貼了7億多塊古瓷片，其中有13,000多個古瓷碗盤、4,000多件古瓷器、400多件漢白玉石雕，可謂極具奢華，是天津的著名地標之一。

Nanfan Stone Archway is a filial piety arch built in the Qing Dynasty (1804). The arch is made of stone with a structure imitating wood. Guzhong Temple is a temple dedicated to the worship of Emperor Yan. The Taizi Hall(太子殿), also known as the Beamless Hall, was built in the Yuan Dynasty (1361), while the rest was constructed during the Ming and Qing Dynasties. 草庵寺 | Cao’an Temple
福建泉州 Quanzhou, Fujian Province

The only surviving Manichaeism(摩尼教) temple in China, Cao’an Temple, originated in the Song Dynasty as a simple grass structure. In the Yuan Dynasty (1339 AD), it was transformed into a stone-structured hip-and gable(歇山式) style building, built against a cliff, exhibiting simplicity and antiquity. It serves as a valuable material basis for studying ancient maritime communication between ancient China and Persia.

胡氏古民居 | Hu Family Ancient Residence
甘肃天水 Tianshui , Gansu Province

The Hu Family Ancient Residence was constructed during the Ming Dynasty (1608-1615) by an official Hu Laijin and inhabited by its descendants. Due to the dry climate in the northwest region, the ancient brick and wood structures have been well-preserved. They are considered a ”rare group of ancient residential buildings with typical Ming Dynasty architectural styles“ nationwide. The existing buildings are divided into the South Residence and the North Residence, comprising eight buildings with a total of twenty-six rooms. The architectural layout, structural design, roof ridge decorations, brick and wood carvings, and more possess high historical, artistic, and scientific value.

description:
What we did in Chiang Mai on 24 October! 

1. Lanterns are being hung all over the city, including at the Wat Phra Singh. The Yi Peng Lantern Festival in Chiang Mai is famous for the sight of thousands of lit lanterns made of paper rising into the night sky. The festival is celebrated on the night of the full moon in the 12th lunar month, which this year falls in November. It’s a shame we won’t be here to experience this magical, romantic and enchanting sight 🏮🌌

2. This is the Three Kings Monument. It shows the three founding fathers of Chiang Mai- King Mengrai, King Ramkhamhaeng and King Ngam Muang 👑🤴👑

3. The entrance to the prayer hall at Wat Dok Euang is so richly decorated. Through the front door you can just about see the golden Buddhas at the main altar ☸️

4. Inside there are lovely murals showing stories of Buddha 🪷

5. We walked all the way to the Ping River which runs through Chiang Mai outside the old city. There were a few hotels, bars and restaurants we saw on the opposite river bank. The Ping river is one of the prime viewing spots during the Yi Peng Lantern Festival to see the lanterns in the sky and floating floral offerings 🏞️

6. The Pung Tao Gong ancestral temple was founded in 1876, but the shrine fell into ruin as the city's Chinese population declined. It was rebuilt during the city’s 700th anniversary celebrations 🇨🇳

7. This is the inside of the new temple, which follows traditional Chinese architecture 🐉

8. The unsuspecting monk in the grounds of Wat Upakhut is in danger of having his head bitten off by the tiger! 🐅

9. Found a number of chickens roaming around Wat Saen Fang. They’re so fluffy it looks like they have trousers on… 🐓

10. Who says money can’t buy you happiness… 🤑

Seeing Traditional Chinese Feng Shui through Traditional Chinese Architecture 
with Jun (E1) 

The traditional Chinese architecture tend to rely on ornaments with auspicious implications for the impressive effect. The ornaments can be inspired by legends, myths or Chinese folk customs etc.

For example, this historical house has a total of 12 swallow tails located neatly on the ridges. Legend has it that in ancient China, it is believed that humans need the blessings of heaven and earth to survive, therefore they respect heaven greatly. The bird on the roof is like an angel – a spiritual creature that can reach heaven and worship Gods. “12” is believed to be an auspicious number.

Feng Shui implementation varies from different cultures and different personal tastes. It is not 
tied to any styles and certainly not to any objects. In order to truly understand the essence of Feng Shui and practice it well, you first must have pretty good understanding of the culture in which Feng Shui originated. You could then use it as a tool to integrate into your own living environment, not just blindly follow the principles.

嘉峪关 | Jiayuguan
甘肃嘉峪关 Jiayuguan , Gansu Province

Jiayuguan, built in 1372 during the Ming Dynasty, is the first major pass at the western end of the Ming Great Wall and a crucial junction on the ancient Silk Road. The inner city is the main structure, constructed with rammed earth. The east and west walls have gate openings, each with a barbican entrance(瓮城). Inside the Jiayuguan inner city wall, there are fourteen structures, including arrow towers, enemy towers, corner towers, pavilions, and gate towers, making it one of the most well-preserved among the many gate cities along the Great Wall.

独乐寺 | Dule Temple
天津 Tianjin

The oldest existing structures in Dule Temple are the Mountain Gate and Guanyin Pavilion（观音阁）, both rebuilt during the Liao Dynasty in 984. The Guanyin Pavilion is the oldest existing wooden pavilion structure(楼阁) in China, constructed to protect the giant statue of Guanyin inside. Its design combines the robustness of the Tang Dynasty with the gracefulness of the Song Dynasty. It is a three-story wooden pavilion with a hidden second floor. Externally, it appears as a two-story structure, with a width of five bays and a depth of four bays. The construction utilized 24 different types of brackets(斗拱) without the use of any nails. Despite experiencing multiple earthquakes throughout history, it still stands tall, making it a marvel in architectural history.

美犹联合救济委员会旧址 | Former Site of American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee
上海 Shanghai

The site building was established in the early 20th century. It is a brick-and-concrete structure, with Corinthian style arch-vaults. The roof is covered with red tiles, and the central facade rises above the roof to form a gable with Baroque style counter-curves. The outer walls are made of blue bricks with decorative red bricks. Between 1937 and 1938, due to the pressures of war, a large number of European Jews poured into Shanghai. The American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee set up a branch here, making this place the "Committee for the Assistance of European Jewish Refugees in Shanghai.”

甘肃敦煌 Dunhuang, Gansu Province

Outside the Chengchengwan(成城湾) Site, there are two pagodas from the Northern Song Dynasty, one large and one small. Both pagodas have undergone severe weathering, with only carvings remaining on the eastern side. The large pagoda is a single-story earth pagoda in a regular octagonal shape. A round-arched door is located on the west side of the pagoda, leading to a small square chamber inside. The four walls and the dome inside the pagoda are adorned with murals. The pagoda's crown has seven layers of lotus flowers sculpted on it.

Chen Guichun Residence is a residential building from the Republic of China era(民国时期), built in 1917. The interiors of the upper and lower levels are also not connected, accessible only by external stairs.

世德堂 | Shide Hall
浙江金华 Jinhua , Zhejiang Province

Shide Hall was built to worship two generals from the Southern Song Dynasty. It features a flush-gable roof, a layout with three courtyards, and is composed of elements such as a screen wall, front hall (gatehouse, stage), front courtyard, two front corridors, middle hall, rear courtyard, two rear corridors, and rear hall. Shide Hall is an important tangible example for the study of the architectural form and traditional building craftsmanship of ancestral halls in Zhejiang. Its brick carvings, wood carvings, and other detailed decorations hold significant artistic value.

胡氏古民居 | Hu Family Ancient Residence
甘肃天水 Tianshui , Gansu Province

The Hu Family Ancient Residence was constructed during the Ming Dynasty (1608-1615) by an official Hu Laijin and inhabited by its descendants. Due to the dry climate in the northwest region, the ancient brick and wood structures have been well-preserved. They are considered a ”rare group of ancient residential buildings with typical Ming Dynasty architectural styles“ nationwide. The existing buildings are divided into the South Residence and the North Residence, comprising eight buildings with a total of twenty-six rooms. The architectural layout, structural design, roof ridge decorations, brick and wood carvings, and more possess high historical, artistic, and scientific value.

Mazha Village is a historical village that harmoniously blends cultural and natural landscapes. Seeing Traditional Chinese Feng Shui through Traditional Chinese Architecture 
with Jun (E1) 

The traditional Chinese architecture tend to rely on ornaments with auspicious implications for the impressive effect. The ornaments can be inspired by legends, myths or Chinese folk customs etc.

For example, this historical house has a total of 12 swallow tails located neatly on the ridges. Legend has it that in ancient China, it is believed that humans need the blessings of heaven and earth to survive, therefore they respect heaven greatly. The bird on the roof is like an angel – a spiritual creature that can reach heaven and worship Gods. “12” is believed to be an auspicious number.

Feng Shui implementation varies from different cultures and different personal tastes. It is not 
tied to any styles and certainly not to any objects. In order to truly understand the essence of Feng Shui and practice it well, you first must have pretty good understanding of the culture in which Feng Shui originated. You could then use it as a tool to integrate into your own living environment, not just blindly follow the principles.

福建泉州 Quanzhou, Fujian Province

Thean Hou Temple, which was Originally built in the Southern Song Dynasty (1196), is the earliest and most grandly structured ancient temple dedicated to Mazu(妈祖). The architectural complex of Tianhou Palace preserves elements from the Song Dynasty and wooden structures from the Ming and Qing Dynasties. The entrance gate is adorned with stone dragon pillars. The layout of the buildings centers around the Tianhou Hall(天后殿), which serves as the main place of worship, extending from north to south. The Tianhou Hall features a multi-eaved, hip-and-gable roof(重檐歇山顶) design, giving the entire structure a tall and majestic appearance, symbolizing the elevated status of Mazu.

法兴寺 | Faxing Temple
山西长治 Changzhi, Shanxi Province

Faxing Temple faces south. The current layout preserves the characteristics of the Tang Dynasty, with a central axis consisting of the mountain gate, relic pagoda(舍利塔), Yuanjue Hall(圆觉殿), and Bodhisattva Hall. The relic pagoda, built in the Tang Dynasty, is a square-plan two-story pavilion-style stone pagoda with corbelled(叠涩) eaves.

开宝寺琉璃塔 | Kaibao Temple Glazed Tile Pagoda
河南开封 Kaifeng, Henan Province

Kaibao Temple Glazed Tile Pagoda is a 13-story octagonal Louge-style(楼阁式) tower. The tower is adorned with red, brown, blue, and green glazed bricks. It is the earliest and tallest extant glazed brick pagoda in China. The tower is embellished with various patterned bricks, featuring over 50 designs such as standing Buddhas, celestial beings, and floral motifs. With its beautiful and lively craftsmanship, it is considered a masterpiece of brick carving art from the Song Dynasty.

“The Red Lantern of Hangzhou: Designing a Sustainable Legacy for the Asian Games”

Located at Zhejiang University of Technology’s Pingfeng Campus, the Asian Games Cricket Field merges modern architectural innovation with deep cultural roots. Inspired by the iconic red lantern, the design celebrates reunion, tradition, and harmony, echoing the charm of Hangzhou while honoring the rich heritage of the campus.

Key Highlights:

. Cultural Symbolism: The use of classic red bricks, known as “Gong Da Red,” integrates the building with the university’s history while reflecting simplicity and cultural depth.

. Architectural Elegance: The “big roof” design combines sharp angles and cantilevered eaves, creating seamless harmony between architecture and the natural surroundings of Ziwu Tide Mountain.

. Eco-Aesthetic Innovation: Drawing inspiration from traditional landscape art, the building incorporates a ceramic brick shell with parametric design, ensuring natural light, ventilation, and an organic connection to its environment.

. Post-Event Sustainability: Beyond the Games, the venue transforms into a multifunctional hub, supporting university activities, conferences, and public engagement while fostering a dynamic campus life.

This cricket field redefines sports architecture by creating a legacy of sustainable design that empowers urban development, connects culture with community, and sets a benchmark for future venues worldwide.

CAMLab Online Seminar

In the early 20th century, with the opening of China and the development of modern industry and trading, Chinese students started to go abroad for education, and introduced modern architecture back into China. But the modernization of Chinese architecture is still neither a clear process nor a definite result usually, and full of contradictions and complexities, the reason of which in turn stems from the contradictious concept of modernity itself.

The lecture, by focusing on the architectural practice in Shanghai by the first architects trained at Penn, will reassess the developing process of Chinese recent modern architecture with a different vision on how to interpret the concept of modernity, and re-examine the influence of Beaux-Arts education on Chinese modern architecture. It will try to promote a better understanding on the overall image of Chinese modern architecture, and suggest potential to integrate it into the broader scope of modern architecture development.

The guest speaker, Tong Ming, is an architectural and urban design professor from the Southeast University in Nanjing, responsible for teaching and research in urban design, urban regeneration, and urban policy analysis. Tong Ming is also the principal architect of TM Studio, a Shanghai based architectural office, and an expert for Shanghai urban planning committee, a member of Academic Committee of Urban Design in the Urban Planning Society of China.

This seminar will be presented with simultaneous translation in English and Mandarin Chinese.  Please register at the link in our bio to join us on Oct 17, 2021 at 9am EST, 9pm CST

China, Guangzhou - Opera House by Zaha Hadid – 2012

The structure in the style of Neo-Futurism was designed by Iraqi architect Zaha Hadid. It is conceived as two rocks washed away by the Pearl River. Its freestanding concrete auditorium set within an exposed granite and glass-clad steel frame took over five years to build, and was praised upon opening by architectural critic Jonathan Glancey in The Guardian, who called it "at once highly theatrical and insistently subtle.”
Neo-futurism is a late-20th/early-21st century architectural style. It evolved out of high-tech architecture, developing many of the same themes and ideas. It is seen as a departure from the more skeptical and referential style of post-modernism, and more of an idealistic approach to the future. It aims to rethink the aesthetics and functionality of rapidly growing urban areas.
The movement has its origins in the mid-20th century structural expressionist work of the Finnish architects Alvar Aalto and Eero Saarinen, as well as the Danish architects Henning Larsen and Jorn Utzon, and other pioneers such as Buckminster Fuller.
Jean-Louis Cohen defined neo-futurism as ‘a corollary to technology, being the structures built today by products of new materials to create previously impossible forms’; whereas, Etan J. Ilfeld has written that neo-futurist aesthetics ‘generates the emergence of artistic modes that would have been impossible prior to computer technology.’
Neo-futurism incorporates urban design that is in touch with human emotions, eco-sustainability, ethical values, and the use of new materials and technologies.
(from Wikipedia)
