China, Guangzhou, Haizhu District – Canton Tower – 2013
Canton Tower was constructed by Guangzhou New Television Tower Group and designed by the Dutch architects Mark Hemel and Barbara Kuit of Information Based Architecture, together with Arup, United Kingdom.
The Canton tower's hyperboloid structure corresponds to the Russian Empire patent No. 1896, dated 12 March 1899 received by Vladimir Shukhov, Russian engineer and architect. The structure is similar to the Adziogol Lighthouse (designed by Shukhov in 1910) in Ukraine's Dnepr delta.
The waist of the tower contains a 180m open-air skywalk where visitors can climb the tower. Outdoor gardens are set within the structure, and at 450m, a large open-air observation deck.
The zone from 80 to 170m features a 4D cinema, a play-hall area, restaurants, coffee shops and outdoor gardens with teahouses. The highest and longest open-air staircase in the world, the Skywalk, starts at 170m and spirals almost 170m higher, all the way through the waist. Skywalk's floors are laid with transparent glass.
The form, volume and structure of the towers is generated by two ellipses, one at foundation level and the other at a horizontal plane at 450m. These two ellipses are rotated relative to another. The tightening caused by the rotation between the two ellipses forms a "waist" halfway up the tower. This means that the lattice structure, which at the bottom of the tower is porous and spacious, becomes denser at waist level. Transparency is reduced and views to the outside are limited. Further up the tower the lattice opens again, accentuated by the tapering of the structural column-tubes. (from Wikipedia)

財神世界大樓, 1991, 嘉義
God of Wealth World Tower, Chiayi, Taiwan

It is said that in front of every Taiwan city's train station, there is a "haunted tower" building. These 15-30-story post-modernist-style commercial buildings symbolize Taiwan's economic bubble around 1990. More akin to casinos than office buildings, they housed stock brokerage firms, hotels, theaters, nightclubs, and market stalls, all thriving under speculative economic conditions. Many significant fires occurred in these buildings during the 1990s.

After the year 2000, Taiwan's economy entered a consolidation phase, and these tall buildings, poorly maintained and managed, gradually became security blind spots, resembling a cyberpunk crime landscape. In the 2020s, they have regained popularity on the internet, and with redevelopment projects around major city stations, they have become targets for urban renewal.

台湾の各都市の駅前には、「幽霊屋敷」と呼ばれる建物があると言われています。これらは約15〜30階で、後現代主義のスタイルの商業ビルで、台湾の1990年前後のバブル経済を象徴しています。これらは商業ビルというよりもむしろカジノであり、投機経済の時代には証券会社、ホテル、映画館、歌劇場、露天商場が満ちていました。1990年代にはこれらの建物で多くの大規模な火災が発生しました。

西暦2000年以降、台湾経済は安定期に入り、これらの高層ビルは保守管理が不足して治安上の難点となり、サイバーパンクのような犯罪の光景が広がりました。2020年代には再びオンラインで注目され、大都市の駅周辺の再開発計画とともに、都市の更新の対象となっています。

China, Guangzhou, Haizhu District – Canton Tower – 2013
Canton Tower was constructed by Guangzhou New Television Tower Group and designed by the Dutch architects Mark Hemel and Barbara Kuit of Information Based Architecture, together with Arup, United Kingdom.
The Canton tower's hyperboloid structure corresponds to the Russian Empire patent No. 1896, dated 12 March 1899 received by Vladimir Shukhov, Russian engineer and architect. The structure is similar to the Adziogol Lighthouse (designed by Shukhov in 1910) in Ukraine's Dnepr delta.
The waist of the tower contains a 180m open-air skywalk where visitors can climb the tower. Outdoor gardens are set within the structure, and at 450m, a large open-air observation deck.
The zone from 80 to 170m features a 4D cinema, a play-hall area, restaurants, coffee shops and outdoor gardens with teahouses. The highest and longest open-air staircase in the world, the Skywalk, starts at 170m and spirals almost 170m higher, all the way through the waist. Skywalk's floors are laid with transparent glass.
The form, volume and structure of the towers is generated by two ellipses, one at foundation level and the other at a horizontal plane at 450m. These two ellipses are rotated relative to another. The tightening caused by the rotation between the two ellipses forms a "waist" halfway up the tower. This means that the lattice structure, which at the bottom of the tower is porous and spacious, becomes denser at waist level. Transparency is reduced and views to the outside are limited. Further up the tower the lattice opens again, accentuated by the tapering of the structural column-tubes. (from Wikipedia)

“The Red Lantern of Hangzhou: Designing a Sustainable Legacy for the Asian Games”

Located at Zhejiang University of Technology’s Pingfeng Campus, the Asian Games Cricket Field merges modern architectural innovation with deep cultural roots. Inspired by the iconic red lantern, the design celebrates reunion, tradition, and harmony, echoing the charm of Hangzhou while honoring the rich heritage of the campus.

Key Highlights:

. Cultural Symbolism: The use of classic red bricks, known as “Gong Da Red,” integrates the building with the university’s history while reflecting simplicity and cultural depth.

. Architectural Elegance: The “big roof” design combines sharp angles and cantilevered eaves, creating seamless harmony between architecture and the natural surroundings of Ziwu Tide Mountain.

. Eco-Aesthetic Innovation: Drawing inspiration from traditional landscape art, the building incorporates a ceramic brick shell with parametric design, ensuring natural light, ventilation, and an organic connection to its environment.

. Post-Event Sustainability: Beyond the Games, the venue transforms into a multifunctional hub, supporting university activities, conferences, and public engagement while fostering a dynamic campus life.

This cricket field redefines sports architecture by creating a legacy of sustainable design that empowers urban development, connects culture with community, and sets a benchmark for future venues worldwide.

China, Guangzhou - Opera House by Zaha Hadid – 2012

The structure in the style of Neo-Futurism was designed by Iraqi architect Zaha Hadid. It is conceived as two rocks washed away by the Pearl River. Its freestanding concrete auditorium set within an exposed granite and glass-clad steel frame took over five years to build, and was praised upon opening by architectural critic Jonathan Glancey in The Guardian, who called it "at once highly theatrical and insistently subtle.”
Neo-futurism is a late-20th/early-21st century architectural style. It evolved out of high-tech architecture, developing many of the same themes and ideas. It is seen as a departure from the more skeptical and referential style of post-modernism, and more of an idealistic approach to the future. It aims to rethink the aesthetics and functionality of rapidly growing urban areas.
The movement has its origins in the mid-20th century structural expressionist work of the Finnish architects Alvar Aalto and Eero Saarinen, as well as the Danish architects Henning Larsen and Jorn Utzon, and other pioneers such as Buckminster Fuller.
Jean-Louis Cohen defined neo-futurism as ‘a corollary to technology, being the structures built today by products of new materials to create previously impossible forms’; whereas, Etan J. Ilfeld has written that neo-futurist aesthetics ‘generates the emergence of artistic modes that would have been impossible prior to computer technology.’
Neo-futurism incorporates urban design that is in touch with human emotions, eco-sustainability, ethical values, and the use of new materials and technologies.
(from Wikipedia)

description:
在上世紀的香港，除鄉郊有仿照或模仿傳統中式建築的樓宇和園林外，市區也有運用這些元素作裝飾的現代建築物。位於彌敦道82至84號的尖沙咀滙豐大廈（HSBC Building Tsim Sha Tsui），便是一例。

尖沙咀滙豐大廈原本名為楊氏大廈（Young’s Building），於1978年落成（8月30日取得佔用許可證，俗稱入伙紙），發展商為時任美麗華酒店集團主席楊志宏私人名下的地產公司美麗都有限公司，建築師是周星樾建築設計有限公司。楊氏大廈取得入伙紙不足一個月，便有新聞（9月10日）報道大廈已給滙豐銀行以一億二千萬元收購，是當時一宗地產大交易。

大廈在彌敦道與金馬倫道交界，佔地6,656平方呎，樓高175.84呎，有一層地庫、低層地下、高層地下，另有十四層及一層在四、五樓之間的機房層。建築物圖則可見三樓及以下的樓層（共6層），起初設計為百貨公司或商舖，四樓（即連接露天平台那層）可用作展覽廳、百貨公司或商舖。滙豐銀行收購大廈後，初時打算把四樓及以下留為己用，樓上則出租為辦公室。

發展商和建築師借用傳統中式城樓及廟宇的輪廓，來粉飾現代西方的巍峨大廈，可算是傳統中式建築「現代化」（modernization）的表面嘗試。不過這種「現代化」只求形似，甚至止於中式建築元素的拼湊運用，未有更高層次的轉化。大廈頂部模仿「宮殿」的上蓋，每層窗戶均有中式屋簷點綴，而基座兩部玻璃升降機的頂部則建造了兩座中式城樓，俯視彌敦道。建築物傳統建築部分的材料由國內運來，並由工藝技術佳的工人負責。

A #stadium #tensilestructure is a type of #architectural design that utilizes tensioned cables or membranes to support the roof or canopy of a stadium or arena. This design approach allows for large, open spans without the need for columns or other support structures, creating a more open and unobstructed space for spectators.
#Tensilestructures are typically made of lightweight materials such as #steel, #aluminum, or #highstrengthfabrics like #PTFE or PVC-coated polyester. The cables or membranes are tensioned between support points to create a stable, yet flexible, structure that can withstand wind, rain, and other environmental factors.
One of the most famous examples of a #stadium #tensilestructure is the Beijing National Stadium, also known as the "Bird's Nest," which was the main venue for the 2008 Olympic Games. The stadium's iconic design features a web-like lattice of steel beams and cables, covered by a translucent #ETFE membrane, creating a striking and functional structure that has become a symbol of #modernChinesearchitecture.

China, Guangzhou - Opera House by Zaha Hadid – 2012

The structure in the style of Neo-Futurism was designed by Iraqi architect Zaha Hadid. It is conceived as two rocks washed away by the Pearl River. Its freestanding concrete auditorium set within an exposed granite and glass-clad steel frame took over five years to build, and was praised upon opening by architectural critic Jonathan Glancey in The Guardian, who called it "at once highly theatrical and insistently subtle.”
Neo-futurism is a late-20th/early-21st century architectural style. It evolved out of high-tech architecture, developing many of the same themes and ideas. It is seen as a departure from the more skeptical and referential style of post-modernism, and more of an idealistic approach to the future. It aims to rethink the aesthetics and functionality of rapidly growing urban areas.
The movement has its origins in the mid-20th century structural expressionist work of the Finnish architects Alvar Aalto and Eero Saarinen, as well as the Danish architects Henning Larsen and Jorn Utzon, and other pioneers such as Buckminster Fuller.
Jean-Louis Cohen defined neo-futurism as ‘a corollary to technology, being the structures built today by products of new materials to create previously impossible forms’; whereas, Etan J. Ilfeld has written that neo-futurist aesthetics ‘generates the emergence of artistic modes that would have been impossible prior to computer technology.’
Neo-futurism incorporates urban design that is in touch with human emotions, eco-sustainability, ethical values, and the use of new materials and technologies.

China, Guangzhou, Haizhu District – Canton Tower – 2013
Canton Tower was constructed by Guangzhou New Television Tower Group and designed by the Dutch architects Mark Hemel and Barbara Kuit of Information Based Architecture, together with Arup, United Kingdom.
The Canton tower's hyperboloid structure corresponds to the Russian Empire patent No. 1896, dated 12 March 1899 received by Vladimir Shukhov, Russian engineer and architect. The structure is similar to the Adziogol Lighthouse (designed by Shukhov in 1910) in Ukraine's Dnepr delta.
The waist of the tower contains a 180m open-air skywalk where visitors can climb the tower. Outdoor gardens are set within the structure, and at 450m, a large open-air observation deck.
The zone from 80 to 170m features a 4D cinema, a play-hall area, restaurants, coffee shops and outdoor gardens with teahouses. The highest and longest open-air staircase in the world, the Skywalk, starts at 170m and spirals almost 170m higher, all the way through the waist. Skywalk's floors are laid with transparent glass.
The form, volume and structure of the towers is generated by two ellipses, one at foundation level and the other at a horizontal plane at 450m. These two ellipses are rotated relative to another. The tightening caused by the rotation between the two ellipses forms a "waist" halfway up the tower. This means that the lattice structure, which at the bottom of the tower is porous and spacious, becomes denser at waist level. Transparency is reduced and views to the outside are limited. Further up the tower the lattice opens again, accentuated by the tapering of the structural column-tubes. (from Wikipedia)

CAMLab Online Seminar

In the early 20th century, with the opening of China and the development of modern industry and trading, Chinese students started to go abroad for education, and introduced modern architecture back into China. But the modernization of Chinese architecture is still neither a clear process nor a definite result usually, and full of contradictions and complexities, the reason of which in turn stems from the contradictious concept of modernity itself.

The lecture, by focusing on the architectural practice in Shanghai by the first architects trained at Penn, will reassess the developing process of Chinese recent modern architecture with a different vision on how to interpret the concept of modernity, and re-examine the influence of Beaux-Arts education on Chinese modern architecture. It will try to promote a better understanding on the overall image of Chinese modern architecture, and suggest potential to integrate it into the broader scope of modern architecture development.

The guest speaker, Tong Ming, is an architectural and urban design professor from the Southeast University in Nanjing, responsible for teaching and research in urban design, urban regeneration, and urban policy analysis. Tong Ming is also the principal architect of TM Studio, a Shanghai based architectural office, and an expert for Shanghai urban planning committee, a member of Academic Committee of Urban Design in the Urban Planning Society of China.

This seminar will be presented with simultaneous translation in English and Mandarin Chinese.  Please register at the link in our bio to join us on Oct 17, 2021 at 9am EST, 9pm CST

China, Guangzhou - Opera House by Zaha Hadid – 2012

The structure in the style of Neo-Futurism was designed by Iraqi architect Zaha Hadid. It is conceived as two rocks washed away by the Pearl River. Its freestanding concrete auditorium set within an exposed granite and glass-clad steel frame took over five years to build, and was praised upon opening by architectural critic Jonathan Glancey in The Guardian, who called it "at once highly theatrical and insistently subtle.”
Neo-futurism is a late-20th/early-21st century architectural style. It evolved out of high-tech architecture, developing many of the same themes and ideas. It is seen as a departure from the more skeptical and referential style of post-modernism, and more of an idealistic approach to the future. It aims to rethink the aesthetics and functionality of rapidly growing urban areas.
The movement has its origins in the mid-20th century structural expressionist work of the Finnish architects Alvar Aalto and Eero Saarinen, as well as the Danish architects Henning Larsen and Jorn Utzon, and other pioneers such as Buckminster Fuller.
Jean-Louis Cohen defined neo-futurism as ‘a corollary to technology, being the structures built today by products of new materials to create previously impossible forms’; whereas, Etan J. Ilfeld has written that neo-futurist aesthetics ‘generates the emergence of artistic modes that would have been impossible prior to computer technology.’
Neo-futurism incorporates urban design that is in touch with human emotions, eco-sustainability, ethical values, and the use of new materials and technologies.

Inspired by the iconic red lantern, the design celebrates reunion, tradition, and harmony, echoing the charm of Hangzhou while honoring the rich heritage of the campus.

Key Highlights:

. Cultural Symbolism: The use of classic red bricks, known as “Gong Da Red,” integrates the building with the university’s history while reflecting simplicity and cultural depth.

. Architectural Elegance: The “big roof” design combines sharp angles and cantilevered eaves, creating seamless harmony between architecture and the natural surroundings of Ziwu Tide Mountain.

. Eco-Aesthetic Innovation: Drawing inspiration from traditional landscape art, the building incorporates a ceramic brick shell with parametric design, ensuring natural light, ventilation, and an organic connection to its environment.

. Post-Event Sustainability: Beyond the Games, the venue transforms into a multifunctional hub, supporting university activities, conferences, and public engagement while fostering a dynamic campus life.

This cricket field redefines sports architecture by creating a legacy of sustainable design that empowers urban development, connects culture with community, and sets a benchmark for future venues worldwide.

Like a prism of gem,
dropped from galaxy,
the skyscraper stands tall.
:
Like a perfect cut of diamond,
the facade stands out on the core.
:
Like a twinkling crystal, the pane reflects the light of day, and the neon in night.
:
Hour by hour, the arrays were set out by plumbing.
Day by day, the mason made its rise floor by floor from datum.
:
Men who drove the piles have been laid in graves when no dirge was sung and no bagpipes were played.
:
Men who topped the building out will no longer enjoy the panoramic view from the roof here in the rest of the life.
And so are the glazers and the men who cleaned up the panes.
:
Praise of the donkeywork is not ever seen on any plaque.
An honourable mention made to worker is hardly ever heard.
:
The skyscraper is for the gorgeous and glorious class
or rather the privileged and bigwigs of the town.
:
Ladies and gentlemen have been in and out of it for years.
It is what the skyscraper reveals, so does the city.
:
The skyscraper proudly reaches for heaven,
but leaves the souls behind.
:
I miss the soul, the reminiscence.
Take a peek at the soul,
when thee walk by it.

description:
📍 IFC Mall, Central, Hong Kong facing the Hong Kong Island skyline⁣
⁣
The Hong Kong skyline is one of the most iconic and breathtaking cityscapes in the world. It is characterized by a mesmerizing blend of modern architectural marvels and traditional Chinese influences. The skyline is dominated by gleaming skyscrapers, with the most famous being the International Commerce Centre (ICC), which stands tall at 1,588 feet, making it the tallest building in Hong Kong.⁣
⁣
In addition to the ICC, other notable skyscrapers that contribute to the stunning skyline include the Bank of China Tower, Central Plaza, and the Two International Finance Centre. These towering structures not only showcase the city's economic prowess but also serve as a testament to its ever-evolving urban landscape.⁣
⁣
Furthermore, the Hong Kong skyline is beautifully complemented by the Victoria Harbour, a natural harbor that separates Hong Kong Island from the Kowloon Peninsula. The harbor serves as a picturesque backdrop, especially during the evening when the buildings light up, creating a dazzling display of colors.⁣
⁣
Overall, the Hong Kong skyline is an architectural wonder that captivates locals and tourists alike. It symbolizes the city's rapid development, economic significance, and unique blend of Eastern and Western influences.⁣
⁣

Hong Kong is the 3rd most important leading international financial centre, after London and New York City. But, did you know that much of it's growth in recent years has been attributed to good feng shui? Because of its geographical location with the mountains behind and waters in front, it is said to be excellent in accordance to feng shui principles. Legend holds that these mountains are home to the dragons that are said to be the bearer of positive and powerful energy. This energy blows through Hong Kong as the dragons make their way from the mountains to the sea to drink and bathe. This is the reason why all the buildings that face the harbour are designed with a gaping hole. So there is no blockage of good energy flow, which ultimately befits the business in the building.

description:
Don’t forget to look up 👆🏼
.
.
It was tempting to follow the Insta-trail and head to one of the photogenic residential complexes in Hong Kong while I was there, but then I asked myself why? It’s not a tourist site, people live there. There were far more interesting things I could spend my time doing.
.
.
I’m not judging those who do go as they may view it as more important than I do, and that’s fine. But I think it’s important not to always #doitforthegram , do it for you. For me, I loved wandering through #mongkok and just happened to find myself in this central block, looked up and there the shot was. .
.

The Jin Yan restaurant at @jhotelshanghaitower Lv 103 - Featuring classic shades of Chinese red, the entrance corridor is made from red glaze and takes inspiration from traditional Chinese architecture. 

Inside, a crystal art installation displays a dragon playing with a pearl, which is considered an auspicious symbol in China. 

The openwork light shades are formed from glaze, and the walls are embellished with jade, glaze and gold foil, while a dragon pattern plays across the marble floor. 

The restaurant has eight private rooms with decorations that incorporate gold, wood, water, fire and earth—the five elements considered by ancient Chinese culture to have built the world. 

It also boasts two special private rooms featuring bespoke artworks from artists in glaze and enamel, each lending their own exceptional touch to the dining experience. 

Painter Zhou Xikang hand-painted landscapes for the moon doors of each private room, inviting diners into a refreshing environment with a feast for both the eyes and the palate.

The Jin Yan restaurant at @jhotelshanghaitower Lv 103 - Featuring classic shades of Chinese red, the entrance corridor is made from red glaze and takes inspiration from traditional Chinese architecture. 

Inside, a crystal art installation displays a dragon playing with a pearl, which is considered an auspicious symbol in China. 

The openwork light shades are formed from glaze, and the walls are embellished with jade, glaze and gold foil, while a dragon pattern plays across the marble floor. 

The restaurant has eight private rooms with decorations that incorporate gold, wood, water, fire and earth—the five elements considered by ancient Chinese culture to have built the world. 

It also boasts two special private rooms featuring bespoke artworks from artists in glaze and enamel, each lending their own exceptional touch to the dining experience. 

Painter Zhou Xikang hand-painted landscapes for the moon doors of each private room, inviting diners into a refreshing environment with a feast for both the eyes and the palate.
